title: IV. A Hymn And A Secret
paragraphs: It was quite late (days are short in November) when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. It was beginning to get dusk. But Alyosha knew he would be admitted without difficulty. Things were managed in our little town as they are everywhere else. At first, of course, once the preliminary inquiry concluded, relatives and a few other people could only obtain interviews with Mitya by going through certain inevitable formalities. But later, though the formalities weren't relaxed, exceptions were made for at least some of Mitya's visitors. So much so that sometimes the meetings with the prisoner in the room set aside for that purpose were practically _tête-à-tête_.

These exceptions, however, were few; only Grushenka, Alyosha, and Rakitin were treated this way. But the captain of police, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably disposed toward Grushenka. His abuse of her at Mokroe weighed on the old man's conscience, and when he learned the whole story, he completely changed his view of her. And, strangely, though he was firmly persuaded of Mitya's guilt, after Mitya was once in prison, the old man came to take a more and more lenient view of him. “He was a man of good heart, perhaps,” he thought, “who had come to grief through drinking and dissipation.” His first horror had given way to pity. As for Alyosha, the police captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin, who had lately taken to coming very often to see the prisoner, was one of the most intimate acquaintances of the “police captain's young ladies,” as he called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent, a scrupulous man in the performance of his duties but kind-hearted. Alyosha, again, had a close long-standing acquaintance with the superintendent, who was fond of talking with him, generally on sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch, and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a great philosopher himself — “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha had an irresistible attraction for him. In the last year the old man had taken to studying the Apocryphal Gospels and was constantly discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit him at the monastery and would spend hours talking with him and with the monks. So even if Alyosha were late at the prison, he had only to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the humblest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. The sentry, of course, didn't trouble him, so long as the authorities were satisfied.

When Mitya was summoned from his cell, he always came downstairs to the room set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered the room, he came upon Rakitin just taking his leave of Mitya. They were both talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw him out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin didn't like running into Alyosha, especially of late. He scarcely spoke to him and bowed to him stiffly. Seeing Alyosha enter now, he frowned and looked away as though entirely absorbed in buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began casting around for his umbrella.
“I mustn't forget my things,” he muttered, just to say something.
“Mind you don't forget other people's things either,” Mitya said as a joke, and laughed at once at his own wit. Rakitin flared up in an instant.
“You'd better offer that advice to your own family, who've always been a slave-driving lot, and not to Rakitin,” he cried, suddenly trembling with anger.

“What's the matter? I was joking,” Mitya cried. “Damn it all — they're all like that!” he turned to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin's hurriedly retreating figure. “He was sitting here laughing and cheerful, and all at once he boils over like that. He didn't even nod to you. Have you broken with him completely? Why are you so late? I haven't just been waiting for you, I've been thirsting for you all morning. But never mind. We'll make up for it now.”
“Why does he come here so often? Surely you two aren't such great friends?” Alyosha asked. He nodded toward the door Rakitin had disappeared through.

“Great friends with Rakitin? No, not that much. Is it likely — a pig like that? He considers me ... a scoundrel. They can't take a joke either, that's the worst of such people. They never get a joke, and their souls are dry, dry and flat; they remind me of the prison walls when I was first brought here. But he's a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it's all over with me now.”
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit down next to him.
“Yes, the trial's tomorrow. Are you really so hopeless, brother?” Alyosha said, with an apprehensive feeling.

“What are you talking about?” Mitya said, looking at him rather uncertainly. “Oh, you mean the trial! Damn it all — until now we've been talking of things that don't matter, about this trial, but I haven't said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial's tomorrow; but it wasn't the trial I meant when I said it was all over with me. Why are you looking at me so critically?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas, ideas, that's all! Ethics! What is ethics?”
“Ethics?” Alyosha asked, wondering.
“Yes — is it a science?”
“Yes, there is such a science ... but ... I admit I can't explain to you what sort of science it is.”

“Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows a lot, damn him! He's not going to be a monk. He means to go to Petersburg. There he'll go in for criticism with an uplifting tendency. Who knows, he may prove useful and make a career for himself too. Ough — they're first-rate, these people, at making careers! Damn ethics. I'm done for, Alexey, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. It makes my heart ache to look at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl. Wait, I made a mistake. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist or something?”
“He must be a savant,” Alyosha answered, “but I admit I can't tell you much about him either. I've heard of him as a savant, but what kind I don't know.”

“Well, damn him, then! I don't know either,” Mitya swore. “A scoundrel of some sort, most likely. They're all scoundrels. And Rakitin will make his way. Rakitin will get on anywhere; he's another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They're all over the place.”
“But what's the matter?” Alyosha asked insistently.

“He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and so launch his literary career. That's what he's coming for; he told me so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to say ‘he couldn't help murdering his father, he was corrupted by his environment,' and so on. He explained it all to me. He's going to give it a tinge of Socialism, he says. But damn the fellow, he can put in a tinge if he likes, I don't care. He can't stand Ivan, he hates him. He's not fond of you either. But I don't turn him out, because he's a clever fellow. Awfully conceited, though. I said to him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren't scoundrels, they're philosophers; all true Russians are philosophers, and though you've studied, you're not a philosopher — you're a vulgar fellow.' He laughed, so maliciously. And I said to him, ‘_De ideabus non est disputandum_.' Isn't that rather good? I can set up for a classicist, you see!” Mitya laughed suddenly.
“Why is it all over with you? You just said so,” Alyosha put in.
“Why is it all over with me? H'm ... The fact is ... taking it as a whole, I'm sorry to lose God — that's why.”
“What do you mean by ‘sorry to lose God'?”

“Imagine: inside, in the nerves, in the head — that is, these nerves are in the brain ... (damn them!) there are kinds of little tails, the little tails of those nerves, and as soon as they start quivering ... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes, and then they start quivering, those little tails ... and when they quiver, an image appears ... it doesn't appear at once, but an instant, a second, passes ... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment — devil take the moment! — but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That's why I see, and then think, because of those tails, not at all because I've got a soul, and because I am some sort of image and likeness. All that's nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply bowled me over. It's magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is arising — that much I understand. And yet I'm sorry to lose God!”
“Well, that's a good thing, anyway,” Alyosha said.

“That I'm sorry to lose God? It's chemistry, brother, chemistry! There's no help for it, your reverence, you'll have to make way for chemistry. And Rakitin does dislike God. Ough — doesn't he dislike Him! That's the sore point with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you preach this in your reviews?' I asked him. ‘Well, if I did it openly, they wouldn't let it through,' he said. He laughed. ‘But what will become of men then?' I asked him. ‘Without God and immortal life? Everything is lawful, they can do whatever they like?' ‘Didn't you know?' he said, laughing. ‘A clever man can do whatever he likes. A clever man knows his way around, but you've put your foot in it, committing a murder, and now you're rotting in prison.' He says that to my face! A regular pig! I used to kick such people out, but now I listen to them. He talks a lot of sense, too. Writes well. He began reading me an article last week. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a minute. Here it is.”
Mitya hurriedly pulled a piece of paper from his pocket and read:
“‘In order to determine this question, it is above all essential to put one's personality in contradiction to one's reality.' Do you understand that?”
“No, I don't,” Alyosha said. He looked at Mitya and listened to him with curiosity.

“I don't understand it either. It's dark and obscure, but intellectual. ‘Everyone writes like that now,' he says, ‘it's the effect of their environment.' They're afraid of the environment. He writes poetry too, the rascal. He's written in honor of Madame Hohlakov's foot. Ha ha ha!”
“I've heard about it,” Alyosha said.
“Have you? And have you heard the poem?”
“No.”

“I've got it. Here it is. I'll read it to you. You don't know — I haven't told you — there's quite a story about it. He's a rascal! Three weeks ago he started teasing me. ‘You've landed yourself in a mess, like a fool, for the sake of three thousand, but I'm going to collar a hundred and fifty thousand. I'm going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.' And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She hadn't much brains in her youth, and now at forty she's lost what she had. ‘But she's awfully sentimental,' he says. ‘That's how I'll get hold of her. Once I marry her, I'll take her to Petersburg and there I'll start a newspaper.' And his mouth was simply watering, the beast — not for the widow, but for the hundred and fifty thousand. And he had me believing it. He came to see me every day. ‘She's coming round,' he declared. He was beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he was turned out of the house. Perhotin's carrying everything before him, bravo! I could kiss the silly old noodle for turning him out of the house. And he had written this doggerel. ‘It's the first time I've soiled my hands with poetry,' he said. ‘It's to win her heart, so it's in a good cause. Once I get hold of the silly woman's fortune, I can be of great social utility.' They have this social justification for every nasty thing they do! ‘Anyway, it's better than your Pushkin's poetry,' he said, ‘because I've managed to advocate enlightenment even in that.' I understand what he means about Pushkin — I can quite see his point, if he really was a man of talent and only wrote about women's feet. But wasn't Rakitin stuck up about his doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! ‘On the convalescence of the swollen foot of the object of my affections' — he came up with that for a title. He's a waggish fellow.
A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come and plasters put, But still they cannot mend her.
Yet, 'tis not for her foot I dread — A theme for Pushkin's muse more fit — It's not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!
For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane — Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!
He's a pig, a regular pig, but he's very arch, the rascal! And he really did work a progressive idea into it. And wasn't he angry when she kicked him out! He was gnashing his teeth!”
“He's already taken his revenge,” Alyosha said. “He's written a paragraph about Madame Hohlakov.”
And Alyosha told him briefly about the paragraph in _Gossip_.

“That's his doing, that's his doing!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That's him! These paragraphs ... I know ... the insulting things that have been written about Grushenka, for instance. And about Katya, too. H'm!”
He paced across the room with a harassed look.

“Brother, I can't stay long,” Alyosha said, after a pause. “Tomorrow will be a great and awful day for you — the judgment of God will be accomplished ... I'm amazed at you — you're walking about here, talking of I don't know what ...”

“No, don't be amazed at me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Am I to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We've talked enough about him. I don't want to say any more about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you'll see. Hush!”
He went up to Alyosha excitedly and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

“Rakitin wouldn't understand it,” he began in a sort of exaltation, “but you, you'll understand it all. That's why I was thirsting for you. You see, there's so much I've been wanting to tell you for ever so long, here, within these peeling walls, but I haven't said a word about what matters most; the moment never seemed to come. Now I can wait no longer. I must pour out my heart to you. Brother, these last two months I've found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden in me, but he'd never have come to the surface if it hadn't been for this blow from heaven. I'm afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I'm not a bit afraid of that — it's something else I'm afraid of now: that that new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer beside me, and I may become friends with him, because even there one may live and love and suffer. One may thaw out and revive a frozen heart in that convict, one may wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature; one may bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we are all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe' at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?' That was a sign to me at that moment. It's for the babe that I'm going. Because we are all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,' because there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.' I go for all, because someone must go for all. I didn't kill father, but I've got to go. I accept it. It's all come to me here, here, within these peeling walls. There are crowds of them there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we'll be in chains and there'll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we'll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it's His privilege — a grand one. Ah, man ought to be dissolved in prayer! What would I be down there without God? Rakitin laughs! If they drive God from the earth, we'll shelter Him underground. One can't exist in prison without God; it's even more impossible than outside prison. And then we men underground will sing from the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”
Mitya was almost gasping for breath as he delivered his wild speech. He turned pale, his lips quivered, and tears rolled down his cheeks.

“Yes, life is full, there is life even underground,” he began again. “You wouldn't believe, Alexey, how I want to live now, what a thirst for existence and consciousness has sprung up in me within these peeling walls. Rakitin doesn't understand that; all he cares about is building a house and renting out flats. But I've been longing for you. And what is suffering? I'm not afraid of it, even if it were beyond reckoning. I'm not afraid of it now. I was afraid of it before. Do you know, perhaps I won't answer at the trial at all. And I feel such strength in me now that I think I could stand anything, any suffering, just so I can say and repeat to myself every moment, ‘I exist.' Through a thousand agonies — I exist. I'm tormented on the rack — but I exist! Though I sit alone atop a pillar — I exist! I see the sun, and even if I don't see the sun, I know it's there. And there's a whole life in that, in knowing that the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan —”
“What of brother Ivan?” Alyosha interrupted, but Mitya didn't hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before, but it was all hidden away in me. It was perhaps just because ideas I didn't understand were surging up in me that I used to drink and fight and rage. It was to stifle them in myself, to still them, to smother them. Ivan is not Rakitin; there is an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx and is silent; he's always silent. It's God that's worrying me. That's the only thing worrying me. What if He doesn't exist? What if Rakitin's right — that it's an idea made up by men? Then if He doesn't exist, man is the chief of the earth, of the universe. Magnificent! Only how is he going to be good without God? That's the question. I always come back to that. For whom is man going to love, then? To whom will he be thankful? To whom will he sing the hymn? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says one can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot can maintain that. I can't understand it. Life's easy for Rakitin. ‘You'd better think about the extension of civic rights,' he tells me, ‘or even about keeping the price of meat down. You'll show your love for humanity more simply and directly that way than by philosophy.' I answered him, ‘Well, but you, without a God, are more likely to raise the price of meat, if it suits you, and make a rouble on every copeck.' He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing with me and another with a Chinaman, so it's a relative thing. Or isn't it? Is it not relative? A treacherous question! You won't laugh if I tell you it's kept me awake two nights. I only wonder now how people can live and think nothing about it. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It's beyond me. But he is silent. I think he's a freemason. I asked him, but he's silent. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul — he was silent. But once he did drop a word.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha took it up quickly.

“I said to him, ‘Then everything is lawful, if it's so?' He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,' he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were right enough.' That's what he let drop. That was all he said. That was going one better than Rakitin.”
“Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he with you?”

“That later; now I have to speak of something else. I haven't said anything about Ivan to you before. I put it off to the last. Once my business here is over and the verdict has been given, then I'll tell you something. I'll tell you everything. We've got something tremendous on our hands. And you shall be my judge in it. But don't start on that now; be silent. You talk of tomorrow, of the trial; but, would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”
“Have you talked to the counsel?”

“What's the use of the counsel? I told him all about it. He's a soft, city-bred rogue — a Bernard! But he doesn't believe me — not a bit of it. Just imagine — he thinks I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,' I asked him, ‘why have you come to defend me?' Hang the lot of them! They've got a doctor down, too, want to prove I'm mad. I won't have that! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do her ‘duty' to the end, whatever the strain!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “The cat! Hard-hearted creature! She knows what I said of her at Mokroe — that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.' They repeated it. Yes, the facts against me have grown as numerous as the sands of the sea. Grigory sticks to his point. Grigory's honest, but a fool. Many people are honest because they're fools: that's Rakitin's idea. Grigory's my enemy. And there are some people who are better as foes than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I'm afraid, oh, I'm afraid she'll tell how she bowed to the ground after that four thousand. She'll pay it back to the last farthing. I don't want her sacrifice; they'll put me to shame at the trial. I wonder how I can stand it. Go to her, Alyosha, ask her not to speak of that in court — can't you? But damn it all, it doesn't matter! I'll get through somehow. I don't pity her. It's her own doing. She deserves what she gets. I'll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why should she have to bear such suffering?” he exclaimed suddenly, with tears. “Grusha's killing me; the thought of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me just now.”
“She told me she was very much grieved by you today.”
“I know. Confound my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry, I kissed her as she was leaving. I didn't ask her forgiveness.”
“Why didn't you?” Alyosha exclaimed.
Suddenly Mitya laughed, almost mirthfully.

“God preserve you, my dear boy, from ever asking forgiveness for a fault from a woman you love. From one you love, especially, however greatly you may have been at fault. Because a woman — the devil only knows what to make of a woman! I know something about them, anyway. But try admitting you're at fault to a woman. Say, ‘I'm sorry, forgive me,' and a shower of reproaches will follow! Nothing will make her forgive you simply and directly; she'll humble you to the dust, bring up things that never happened, recall everything, forget nothing, add things of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best, the best of them do it. She'll scrape up all the scrapings and heap them on your head. They're ready to flay you alive, I tell you, every one of them, all these angels without whom we can't live! I tell you plainly and openly, dear boy, every decent man ought to be under some woman's thumb. That's my conviction — not conviction, but feeling. A man ought to be magnanimous, and it's no disgrace to a man! No disgrace to a hero, not even a Caesar! But don't ever beg her pardon, all the same, for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who's come to ruin through women. No, I'd better make it up to Grusha somehow without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, worship her. Only she doesn't see it. No, she still thinks I don't love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! In the past it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me, but now I've taken all of her soul into my soul, and through her I've become a man myself. Will they marry us? If they don't, I'll die of jealousy. I imagine something every day. What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha repeated all that Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him repeat things, and seemed pleased.

“Then she's not angry at my being jealous?” he exclaimed. “She's a regular woman! ‘I've a fierce heart myself!' Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can't bear anyone's being jealous of me. I can't stand it. We'll fight. But I'll love her, I'll love her infinitely. Will they marry us? Do they let convicts marry? That's the question. And without her I can't exist ...”
Mitya walked frowning across the room. It was almost dark. He suddenly seemed terribly worried.

“So there's a secret, she says, a secret? We've cooked up a plot against her, and Katya is mixed up in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that's not it. You're very wide of the mark, in your foolish feminine way. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I'll tell you our secret!”

He glanced around, went close up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered to him with an air of mystery, though in reality no one could hear them: the old warder was dozing in the corner, and not a word could reach the ears of the soldiers on guard.

“I'll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered hurriedly. “I meant to tell you later, because how could I decide anything without you? You're everything to me. Though I say Ivan is superior to us, you are my angel. It's your decision that will decide it. Perhaps it's you who are superior and not Ivan. You see, it's a question of conscience, a question of the higher conscience — the secret is so important that I can't settle it myself, and I've put it off until I could speak to you. But even so, it's too early to decide now, because we must wait for the verdict. As soon as the verdict is given, you'll decide my fate. Don't decide it now. I'll tell you now. You listen, but don't decide. Stand there and keep quiet. I won't tell you everything. I'll only tell you the idea, without the details, and you keep quiet. Not a question, not a movement. You agree? But, goodness, what shall I do with your eyes? I'm afraid your eyes will tell me your decision, even if you don't speak. Oo — I'm afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan is suggesting that I _escape_. I won't tell you the details: it's all been thought through, it can all be arranged. Hush, don't decide. I'd go to America with Grusha. You know I can't live without Grusha! What if they won't let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha what would I be doing there underground with a hammer? I'd only smash my own skull with the hammer! But on the other hand — my conscience? I'd have run away from suffering. A sign has come, I reject the sign. I have a way of salvation and I turn my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the goodwill,' I can be of more use than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What's America? America is vanity again! And there's plenty of swindling in America too, I expect. I'd have run away from crucifixion! I tell you, you know, Alexey, because you're the only person who can understand this. There's no one else. It's folly, madness to others, all that I've told you about the hymn. They'll say I'm out of my mind or a fool. I'm not out of my mind and I'm not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he doesn't answer — he doesn't speak. He doesn't believe in the hymn. Don't speak, don't speak. I see how you look! You've already decided. Don't decide, spare me! I can't live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”
Mitya finished beside himself. He held Alyosha with both hands on his shoulders, his yearning, feverish eyes fixed on his brother's.
“They don't let convicts marry, do they?” he repeated for the third time in a pleading voice.
Alyosha listened with extreme surprise and was deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very keen on it, and whose idea was it?”

“His, his, and he's very keen on it. He didn't come to see me at first, then he suddenly came a week ago and launched straight into it. He's awfully keen. He doesn't ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I'll obey him, even though I laid open my whole heart to him the way I have to you, and told him about the hymn, too. He told me he'd arrange it; he's found out about everything. But of that later. He's simply set on it. It's all a matter of money: he'll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says we can arrange a magnificent escape for ten thousand.”
“And he told you on no account to tell me?” Alyosha asked again.
“To tell no one, and especially not you; on no account to tell you. He's afraid, no doubt, that you'd stand before me as my conscience. Don't tell him I told you. Don't tell him, for anything.”

“You're right,” Alyosha pronounced. “It's impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you'll decide for yourself. Then you'll find that new man in yourself and he will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who'll decide _à la_ Bernard — because I think I'm a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.
“But, brother, have you no hope, then, of being acquitted?”

Mitya shrugged his shoulders nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it's time you were going,” he said, with sudden haste. “There's the superintendent shouting in the yard. He'll be here in a moment. We're late; it's irregular. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Sign me with the cross, darling, for the cross I have to bear tomorrow.”
They embraced and kissed.
“Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “suggests my escaping; but, of course, he believes I did it.”
A mournful smile came to his lips.
“Have you asked him whether he believes it?” Alyosha asked.
“No, I haven't. I wanted to, but I couldn't. I hadn't the courage. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-bye!”
Once more they kissed hurriedly, and Alyosha was just on his way out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

“Stand facing me! That's right!” And again he seized Alyosha, putting both hands on his shoulders. His face suddenly went quite pale, so that it was dreadfully visible even in the gathering darkness. His lips twitched, his eyes locked on Alyosha.
“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as you would before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you in yourself, believe it? The whole truth — don't lie!” he cried desperately.
Everything seemed to heave in front of Alyosha, and he felt something like a stab at his heart.
“Hush! What do you mean?” he faltered helplessly.
“The whole truth, the whole, don't lie!” Mitya repeated.
“I've never for one instant believed that you were the murderer!” broke in a shaking voice from Alyosha's chest, and he raised his right hand in the air, as though calling God to witness his words.
Mitya's whole face lit up with bliss.

“Thank you!” he said slowly, as though letting out a sigh after a faint. “Now you've given me new life. Would you believe it, till this moment I've been afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well — go! You've given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Go on — go! Love Ivan!” was Mitya's last word.

Alyosha went out in tears. Such distrust in Mitya, such a lack of confidence even toward him, toward Alyosha — all of it suddenly opened up before Alyosha an unsuspected depth of hopeless grief and despair in the soul of his unhappy brother. Intense, infinite compassion overwhelmed him in an instant. There was a poignant ache in his torn heart. “Love Ivan!” — he suddenly recalled Mitya's words. And he was going to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He was as worried about Ivan as about Mitya, and more so than ever now.
